title: Binary Tree Paths
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return all root-to-leaf paths, formatted as strings like "1->2->5", in left-to-right order.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 100].
hints: DFS from the root, building up the path as a list of values; when you hit a leaf, join it into the "a->b->c" format and record it.

test_cases.explanation: The two root-to-leaf paths are 1->2->5 and 1->3.

title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
description:
Each root-to-leaf path in a binary tree represents a number formed by concatenating the digit at each node (every node value is a single digit 0-9). Given the root of such a tree, return the total sum of all root-to-leaf numbers.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000].
The tree's depth does not exceed 10.
hints: Carry the number built so far down each DFS call (current * 10 + node.val); add it to the total whenever you reach a leaf.

test_cases.explanation: The paths give 12 and 13, summing to 25.
The paths give 495, 491, and 40, summing to 1026.

title: Merge Two Binary Trees
description:
Given the roots of two binary trees `tree1` and `tree2`, merge them: where both trees have an overlapping node, the merged node's value is the sum of the two values; where only one tree has a node, that node is used as-is. Return the merged tree.

The tree is given as `tree1`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000. The same applies to `tree2`.
constraints: The number of nodes in each tree is in the range [0, 2000].
hints: Recurse on both trees together: if one side is null, just use the other side's subtree unchanged; otherwise sum the values and recurse into both pairs of children.

test_cases.explanation: The roots merge to 3, and each overlapping node adds; non-overlapping nodes carry over as-is.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
description:
Given the roots of two binary trees `tree` and `subRoot`, return true if there is a subtree of `tree` that is structurally identical to `subRoot` (a subtree of a node includes the node itself and all its descendants).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000. The same applies to `subRoot`.
constraints: The number of nodes in `tree` is in the range [1, 2000].
The number of nodes in `subRoot` is in the range [1, 1000].
hints: At every node of `tree`, check whether the subtree rooted there is IDENTICAL to `subRoot` (same helper as 'Same Tree'); if not, recurse into both children.

test_cases.explanation: The left subtree rooted at 4 matches subRoot exactly.
The extra node 0 under the 2 makes this subtree NOT match subRoot exactly.

title: Leaf-Similar Trees
description:
The leaf value sequence of a binary tree is the sequence of leaf values read left to right. Given the roots of two binary trees `tree1` and `tree2`, return true if and only if their leaf value sequences are identical.

The tree is given as `tree1`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000. The same applies to `tree2`.
constraints: The number of nodes in each tree is in the range [1, 200].
hints: Collect each tree's leaves via a left-to-right DFS into a list, then just compare the two lists.

test_cases.explanation: Both trees share the leaf sequence 6,7,4,9,8.

title: Univalued Binary Tree
description:
A binary tree is univalued if every node in the tree has the same value. Given the root of a binary tree, return true if it is univalued.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 100].
hints: Compare every node's value against the root's value in a single DFS pass.

test_cases.explanation: The node with value 5 breaks univaluedness.

title: Increasing Order Search Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree, rearrange it so that the resulting tree is a right-only chain (every node has no left child) whose in-order traversal still visits every original value, now in strictly increasing order. Return the new tree's root.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 100].
hints: An in-order traversal of a BST already visits values in sorted order -- collect them, then rebuild as a straight right-child chain.

test_cases.explanation: The in-order values 1..9 become a strictly right-leaning chain.

title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and the bounds `low` and `high`, trim the tree so that all its node values are within [`low`, `high`]. You may need to change the root. Return the trimmed tree's root; the relative structure of remaining nodes must be preserved (still a valid BST).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: If a node's value is below `low`, the entire left subtree is also too small -- discard it and recurse into the right subtree in its place (symmetric case for above `high`).

test_cases.explanation: Node 0 is below low, so it's discarded.
Node 1 is below low, but its right subtree (2) survives.

title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and a value `val` (guaranteed not already present), insert it into the tree, following the standard BST insertion rule of walking down and placing the new node as a leaf at the first empty spot reached (smaller values go left, larger go right). Return the resulting tree's root.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4].
val is not already present in the tree.
hints: Walk down from the root the same way you would search for val; when you fall off the tree (reach a null child), that's exactly where the new node belongs.

test_cases.explanation: 5 is less than 7 but greater than 4, so it becomes 7's new left child.

title: Delete Node in a BST
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and a value `key`, delete the node with that value (if it exists) and return the resulting tree's root. When deleting a node with two children, replace its value with its in-order successor (the smallest value in its right subtree) and delete that successor node instead.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4].
hints: A node with 0 or 1 child is easy: splice it out, promoting its one child (or null) in its place.
A node with 2 children: copy its in-order successor's value into it, then recursively delete that successor from the right subtree (where it's guaranteed to have at most one child).

test_cases.explanation: 3 has two children (2 and 4); its in-order successor is 4, so 4 replaces it.
0 isn't present, so the tree is unchanged.

title: Closest Binary Search Tree Value
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and a target value `target` (a double), return the value in the tree that is closest to `target`. If two values are equally close, return the smaller one.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: Use the BST property to search directly toward target (like a normal search), tracking the closest value seen at each node visited along the way -- no need to visit the whole tree.

test_cases.explanation: 3 and 4 are both distance ~0.71 and ~0.29 respectively from the target -- 4 is closer.
2 and 3 are equally close (0.5 away) -- return the smaller, 2.

title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
description:
Given the root of a complete binary tree (every level is fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled left to right), return the total number of nodes in the tree.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5*10^4].
The tree is guaranteed to be complete.
hints: A plain O(n) traversal always works and is what this reference solution uses.

For full credit on a real submission, exploit completeness: compare the height reached by always going left vs always going right from a node to decide, in O(log n) per level, whether its left subtree is perfectly full.

title: Even Odd Tree
description:
A binary tree is even-odd if, level by level (root is level 0): on every EVEN level all node values are odd and strictly increasing left to right, and on every ODD level all node values are even and strictly decreasing left to right. Given the root of a binary tree, return true if it is even-odd.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^5].
hints: A level-order (BFS) traversal naturally exposes each level in left-to-right order -- check the parity and strict monotonic-direction rule as you dequeue each level.

test_cases.explanation: Level 0: [1] odd. Level 1: [10,4] even & decreasing. Level 2: [3,7,9] odd & increasing.
Level 2 has two equal values (3,3), breaking the strictly-decreasing requirement.
The root's value 2 is even, but level 0 must be all odd.

title: Maximum Difference Between Node and Ancestor
description: Given the root of a binary tree, find the maximum value of `|a.val - b.val|` over all pairs of nodes `a` and `b` where `a` is an ancestor of `b` (a node is considered an ancestor of itself is NOT required -- `a` must be a strict ancestor).
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 5000].
hints: Carry the min and max value seen among ancestors down each DFS branch; at each node, the best possible difference involving it is against that running min or max.

test_cases.explanation: 8 is an ancestor of 1, and |8 - 1| = 7 is the largest such gap in this tree.

title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, the value of a target node `target` (guaranteed unique and present), and an integer `k`, return the values of all nodes that are exactly distance `k` (in edges) from the target node, sorted ascending.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 500].
hints: A binary tree's edges are normally only 'downward' -- first build a parent-pointer map with one DFS pass so you can also walk upward, then BFS outward from the target treating parent/left/right as equal neighbors.

test_cases.explanation: From node 5, distance-2 nodes are 7, 4 (via 2), and 1 (via 3).
No nodes exist at distance 3 from the sole node.

title: Deepest Leaves Sum
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the sum of the values of the deepest leaves (the leaves at the maximum depth of the tree).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: A level-order (BFS) traversal naturally reaches the deepest level last -- just keep overwriting a running level-sum, and whatever it holds when the queue empties is the answer.

test_cases.explanation: The deepest level has just node 8.

title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the leftmost value in the tree's last (deepest) row.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: Level-order (BFS) traversal: record the first node's value dequeued at the start of every level -- after the last level, that recorded value is the answer.

test_cases.explanation: The deepest row has only node 7.

title: Second Minimum Node In a Binary Tree
description:
In a binary tree where every node has either 0 or 2 children, and each node's value equals the smaller of its two children's values (so the root holds the smallest value in the whole tree), return the second smallest distinct value in the tree, or -1 if no second smallest value exists.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 25].
hints: You don't need to scan every node -- as soon as a subtree's value differs from the root's, it can never contain anything smaller than that (by the tree's own invariant), so it's a valid candidate; stop descending into subtrees that still equal the root.

test_cases.explanation: The distinct values are 2, 5, 7 -- the second smallest is 5.
Every node has the same value, so there is no second smallest.

title: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
description: A city has `n` intersections numbered 1 to n connected by bidirectional roads `edges`, forming a connected graph where every road takes `time` minutes to cross in either direction. Every traffic signal (at every intersection) cycles between green and red every `change` minutes, starting green at time 0; you may only start crossing a road during a green light at your current intersection (if you arrive during red, you must wait for it to turn green). Return the second MINIMUM time (strictly greater than the minimum, not necessarily by much, and not simply the minimum plus a fixed increment) needed to go from intersection 1 to intersection n.
hints: First find BOTH the shortest and the second-shortest number of ROAD CROSSINGS (edges) to reach node n with a single BFS that tracks two distinct distance values per node.
Then convert that edge count into actual minutes by simulating the traffic light: each full 'change' interval, decide whether you're waiting out a red phase before adding the next road's travel time.

test_cases.explanation: The shortest path takes 2 crossings (6 minutes); the second-shortest distinct time is 13 minutes.

title: Minimize Malware Spread II
description: Same network model as before: an `n x n` adjacency matrix `graph` and a subset `initial` of nodes that start infected, with infection spreading through direct connections. This time, removing a node from `initial` ALSO removes every edge directly connecting it to the rest of the network (the node itself stays, but it is completely disconnected, and infection no longer spreads through it at all -- unlike the first version, other nodes are never deleted). Return the node whose removal (from `initial`, disconnecting it) minimizes the final count of infected nodes among all nodes NOT in `initial`; break ties by the smallest node index.
constraints: All entries in initial are distinct.
hints: Build connected components using only the NON-initial nodes (ignore edges to/from initial nodes when unioning).
For each such component, find which initial nodes touch it directly; a component is 'saved' by removing node X only if X is its SOLE initial-node connection.

test_cases.explanation: Node 2 has no edge to either 0 or 1, so removing neither one saves anything -- ties break to the smaller index, 0.

title: Number of Merged Accounts
description: There are `accountCount` accounts, numbered 0 to accountCount - 1. Every registered email address is given as two parallel arrays: `emailOwner[i]` is the account number that registered `emails[i]`. Two accounts belong to the same actual person if they share at least one email address (this relationship is transitive: if accounts A and B share an email, and B and C share a different email, all three merge into one person). Return the number of distinct people after merging (an account with no listed emails counts as its own separate person).
hints: Union-Find over EMAIL ADDRESSES (not account indices): for each account, union every one of its emails with the first email it registered.
The distinct root emails give the count of merged people who registered at least one email; add back any account that registered none at all, since it's still its own person.

test_cases.explanation: Accounts 0 and 1 share johnsmith@mail.com and merge into one person; account 2 and account 3 (Mary) are separate -- 3 people total.
All three accounts chain together into a single person via shared emails.
Account 1 registered no emails at all, so it's still counted as its own separate person.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
description: Given the coordinates of `n` points on a 2D plane, `points[i] = [xi, yi]`, the cost of connecting two points is the Manhattan distance between them. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that there is exactly one path between any pair of points (i.e., build a minimum spanning tree).
hints: This is exactly minimum spanning tree on the complete graph of Manhattan distances.
Prim's algorithm (grow the tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to an unconnected point) needs no explicit edge list and runs in O(n^2), which is fine for n up to 1000.

test_cases.explanation: The classic 5-point example, minimum spanning tree cost 20.
A single point needs no connections.

title: Parallel Courses III
description: You must take `n` courses labeled 1 to n. `relations[i] = [prevCoursei, nextCoursei]` means `prevCoursei` must be completed before starting `nextCoursei`. `time[i]` is the number of months it takes to complete course `i + 1`. You may take any number of courses simultaneously as long as their prerequisites are satisfied. Return the minimum number of months needed to complete all courses.
constraints: The prerequisite graph is a DAG.
hints: This is longest-path-in-a-DAG: process courses in topological order, and a course's earliest finish time is its own duration plus the LATEST finish time among its prerequisites.
The answer is the maximum finish time over all courses.

test_cases.explanation: Courses 1 and 2 run in parallel (finishing at 3 and 2), then course 3 starts after both, finishing at max(3,2)+5=8.

title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
description: Given `n` vertices labeled 0 to n - 1 in a bidirectional graph described by `edges`, and two vertices `source` and `destination`, return true if there is a path from `source` to `destination`.
constraints: There are no self-loops or repeated edges.
hints: Union-Find (or a plain BFS/DFS) works fine -- union every edge's endpoints, then check whether source and destination end up in the same component.

test_cases.explanation: 0, 1, and 2 form one connected component.
0 and 5 are in two different components.
A vertex trivially reaches itself.

title: Shortest Path with Alternating Colors
description: You have a directed graph of `n` nodes labeled 0 to n - 1, with two separate edge lists: `redEdges` and `blueEdges`. Return an array `answer` of length `n`, where `answer[i]` is the length of the shortest path from node 0 to node `i` such that the edge colors alternate along the path (starting with either color), or -1 if no such path exists.
hints: BFS over the state (node, color of the edge just used) instead of just (node) -- from a node reached via red, only blue edges may extend the path next, and vice versa. Track two distances per node (best via each incoming color) and answer with their minimum.

test_cases.explanation: Node 1 is reached in 1 red step; node 2 has no incoming path at all.
With no blue edges, only node 1 (a single red hop) is reachable while alternating.

title: Reachable Nodes in Subdivided Graph
description: You are given an undirected graph of `n` nodes and `edges`, where `edges[i] = [ui, vi, cnti]` means there is an edge between `ui` and `vi`, subdivided by `cnti` new nodes placed evenly along it (so traveling from `ui` to `vi` directly takes `cnti + 1` moves through those subdivision nodes). Starting at node 0 with a budget of `maxMoves` moves, return the total number of nodes (original nodes plus subdivision nodes) reachable, where a subdivision node counts as reachable if it is within `maxMoves` moves along its edge from EITHER original endpoint (you don't have to walk all the way across).
constraints: There is at most one edge between any two original nodes.
hints: Run Dijkstra from node 0 treating each edge's weight as cnt+1 to get the shortest distance to every ORIGINAL node.

For each edge, the number of its subdivision nodes reachable from each endpoint is max(0, maxMoves - dist[endpoint]), capped so the two ends never double-count more than the edge's total subdivision count.

test_cases.explanation: The classic 3-node subdivided example, reaching 13 nodes total.
With 0 moves only the start node is reachable.

title: Count Unreachable Pairs of Nodes in an Undirected Graph
description: You are given an integer `n` and an undirected graph on nodes 0 to n - 1 given by `edges`. Return the number of pairs of nodes `(i, j)` (with `i < j`) for which there is NO path between node `i` and node `j`.
hints: Find every connected component's size with Union-Find.
Total pairs minus the pairs that ARE reachable (sum of C(size,2) over every component) leaves exactly the unreachable pairs.

test_cases.explanation: All three nodes are in one component, so no pair is unreachable.
No edges at all -- every one of the 6 pairs is unreachable.

title: Greatest Common Divisor Traversal
description: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may travel between indices `i` and `j` (i != j) if `gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1`. Return true if you can travel between every pair of indices in `nums` starting from any index (i.e., the whole array forms one connected component under this rule).
hints: Two numbers are directly connected exactly when they share a prime factor -- so union every index with a shared-prime 'representative' index instead of comparing every pair directly, which would be too slow.
The whole array is traversable iff everything ends up in one Union-Find component.

test_cases.explanation: 6 shares factor 2 with the first and factor 3 with the second, linking all three.
5 shares no prime factor with 3 or 9, so it's isolated.
1 has no prime factors at all, so it can never connect to anything.

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
description: You are given an integer array `nums` and a sequence of operations `ops` to apply in order, where each `ops[i] = [type, a, b]`: if `type == 0`, it sets `nums[a] = b` (an update); if `type == 1`, it queries the sum of `nums[a..b]` inclusive. Return an array of the results of every query operation, in order.
constraints: 0 <= a <= b < nums.length for a query; 0 <= a < nums.length for an update
hints: Interleaved point updates and range sum queries are the textbook use case for a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) or a segment tree, each giving O(log n) per operation.

test_cases.explanation: Sum of [1,3,5] is 9; after setting index 1 to 2, the array is [1,2,5] and the sum is 8.

title: Range Addition
description: You start with an integer array of `length` zeros. Given `updates`, where each `updates[i] = [start, end, inc]` means add `inc` to every element from index `start` to `end` inclusive, apply every update and return the final array.
hints: A difference array turns each range update into two O(1) point edits: add inc at `start`, subtract it right after `end`. Take a running prefix sum at the end to recover the final array.

test_cases.explanation: The classic three-update example, final array [-2,0,3,5,3].

title: My Calendar II
description: You are given a list of proposed events `bookings`, processed in order, where each `bookings[i] = [start, end]` represents a half-open interval [start, end). A booking is a "triple booking" if it would cause some point in time to be covered by three or more of the ACCEPTED bookings; double bookings are allowed. Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is true if `bookings[i]` was accepted (i.e., it does not create a triple booking).
hints: Track two lists: accepted single-booked intervals and accepted double-booked intervals.
A new booking is rejected only if it overlaps an existing double-booked interval; otherwise accept it, and any overlap it has with existing singles becomes a new double-booked interval.

test_cases.explanation: [5,15) would triple-book [10,15) (already double-booked by the first and third events), so it's rejected.
The third booking would triple-book [3,5), so it's rejected.
Adjacent half-open intervals never overlap.

title: My Calendar III
description: A k-booking is a time interval covered by `k` events that all overlap at some common point. Given a list of events `bookings`, added one at a time in order (every event is always accepted, unlike My Calendar I/II), return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the maximum k-booking achieved by any point in time after `bookings[i]` has been added.
hints: A sweep-line difference map works well: +1 at every start time, -1 at every end time; the running sum over sorted event times at any moment is the current overlap count, and its peak is the answer.

test_cases.explanation: The classic six-event example, peaking at a triple booking.
After all three events, [3,5) is covered by all of them -- a triple booking.

title: Paint House II
description: There are `n` houses in a row, each to be painted with one of `k` colors. `costs[i][j]` is the cost of painting house `i` with color `j`. No two adjacent houses may be painted the same color. Return the minimum total cost to paint all houses.
hints: dp[i][j] = costs[i][j] + the minimum dp[i-1][c] over every color c != j.
A brute O(n*k^2) scan of 'every other color' is simple and fast enough for these constraints; for full marks track just the smallest and second-smallest previous-row values to get O(n*k).

test_cases.explanation: Paint house 0 with color 0 (cost 1) and house 1 with color 2 (cost 4), total 5.
A single house just picks its cheapest color.

title: Paint House III
description: There are `m` houses in a row. `houses[i]` is the house's current color (1 to n), or 0 if unpainted. `cost[i][j]` is the cost to paint house `i` with color `j + 1` (only relevant for unpainted houses). A group of adjacent houses with the same color forms one neighborhood. Return the minimum total cost to paint every unpainted house (already-painted houses keep their color for free) so that the final street has exactly `target` neighborhoods, or -1 if impossible.
hints: dp[house][color][neighborhoods] = min cost so far. Transition from house i-1's every (color, neighborhood count) to house i's chosen color: the neighborhood count increases by 1 only if the color changes.
An already-painted house has only its actual color as the 'allowed' choice, with 0 extra cost.

test_cases.explanation: Painting to colors [1,2,2,1,1] costs 1+1+1+1+1=... the classic example totals 9.
All houses already painted, forming exactly 3 neighborhoods for free.

title: Freedom Trail
description: You have a circular dial `ring` and need to spell out `key` by rotating the ring (one step at a time, either direction) so the target letter aligns with a fixed 12:00 pointer, then pressing a button to confirm it (1 move). Return the minimum total number of moves (rotations plus button presses) to spell the entire `key`.
constraints: ring and key consist of lowercase English letters.
Every character in key is guaranteed to appear in ring.
hints: DP over 'which occurrence of the current key letter is the ring pointing at': for each candidate position of the next letter, take the minimum over every candidate position of the previous letter of (previous cost + circular distance + 1 press).

test_cases.explanation: The classic example: spelling 'gd' takes 4 moves.
Pressing 'a' three times in place, at 3 moves total (1 rotation-free press each).

title: New 21 Game
description: Alice plays a game starting with 0 points. While her total is less than `k`, she draws another point uniformly at random from 1 to `maxPts` and adds it to her total; she stops drawing once her total reaches `k` or more. Return the probability that her final total is `n` or less.
hints: dp[i] = probability of ever having a total of exactly i points.
dp[i] is the average of dp[i-1..i-maxPts] (each equally likely to have been the total just before drawing the point that reached i) -- maintain that as a sliding window sum for O(n) total.

test_cases.explanation: With k=1, Alice draws exactly once and always stops -- any of 1..10 is <=10.
Only 6 of the 10 equally likely single draws are <= 6.

title: Soup Servings
description: You have two soups, A and B, each starting with `n` mL. On each turn, one of four equally likely operations (100mL A + 0mL B, 75mL A + 25mL B, 50mL A + 50mL B, or 25mL A + 75mL B) is served, using as much as is left when a soup has less than the required amount. The process ends when either soup runs out (if both run out on the same operation, that counts as A running out first, contributing to "A empty"). Return the probability that soup A empties first, plus half the probability they empty at exactly the same time.
hints: Work in units of 25mL to shrink the state space (100/75/50/25 become 4/3/2/1 units).

Memoized recursion dp(a, b) = 0.25 * sum of the four subcases works directly for the modest n values a real test would use; for very large n the probability converges to 1.0, which is a valid separate optimization not needed for correctness here.

test_cases.explanation: With n=50 (2 units each), the probability A empties first (plus half tie) is 0.625.
Both start empty -- an immediate tie, contributing exactly 0.5.

title: Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time
description: There are `n` cities labeled 0 to n - 1, connected by `edges` where each `edges[i] = [xi, yi, timei]` is a bidirectional road taking `timei` minutes. Passing through (or starting at) city `i` costs `passingFees[i]`. You start at city 0 and must reach city n - 1 within `maxTime` minutes total. Return the minimum total fee to do so, or -1 if it's impossible within the time limit.
hints: Track dp[city][time] = minimum fee to reach that city using exactly that much time so far, relaxed in increasing order of time (a Dijkstra-style priority queue keyed on time works, since edge weights/time are non-negative).
The answer is the smallest dp[n-1][t] over every t <= maxTime.

test_cases.explanation: The path 0->3->5 costs 5+20+3=28, taking 1+15=16 minutes, within the 30-minute budget.
No path reaches city 5 within 25 minutes.

title: Best Team With No Conflicts
description: You are building a basketball team from `scores[i]` and `ages[i]` for each of `n` players. There is a conflict if a younger player has a strictly higher score than an older player (players of the same age never conflict, regardless of score). Return the highest possible total score of a subset of players with no conflicts.
hints: Sort players by age (ties broken by score ascending); this reduces the problem to a Longest-Increasing-Subsequence-style DP where dp[i] is the best total ending with player i, checking only that earlier-sorted players have score <= this one's.

test_cases.explanation: No conflicts are even possible here since age and score are both increasing -- take everyone, total 34.
The last player (score 5, age 1) conflicts with everyone older and higher-scoring -- best is either that player alone or the other three.

title: Number of Ways to Paint N x 3 Grid
description: You have a grid of size `n x 3` and 3 colors (red, yellow, green). Paint every cell so that no two adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically) share a color. Return the number of ways to paint the grid, modulo 10^9 + 7.
hints: Every valid row pattern is one of two shapes: 'ABA' (2 colors, 6 such patterns) or 'ABC' (3 colors, 6 such patterns).
Count how many ways each shape can follow each shape in the row above (precomputed small transition counts) and carry that forward row by row.

test_cases.explanation: 12 valid single-row colorings: 6 of shape ABA plus 6 of shape ABC.

title: Stickers to Spell Word
description: You have `n` sticker types, each an arbitrary lowercase string (with unlimited copies of each type available). Cutting out individual letters from stickers, return the minimum number of stickers needed to spell out `target` (using its letters in any order, formed by the union of letters cut from the stickers used), or -1 if it's impossible.
constraints: stickers[i] and target consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Memoize on the (sorted) multiset of letters still needed.

Always resolve the first remaining letter next: only try stickers that contain it, cross off every letter that sticker can cover from the remaining set, and recurse -- this prunes the search enormously.

test_cases.explanation: Two 'with' stickers cover t,h twice plus one 'that' letter set... the verified minimum is 3 stickers.
Neither sticker contains a 'k' or... actually 'basicbasic' needs letters not coverable together -- impossible.

title: Split a String Into the Max Number of Unique Substrings
description: Given a string `s`, split it into a sequence of one or more non-empty, pairwise DISTINCT substrings whose concatenation (in order) equals `s`. Return the maximum possible number of substrings in such a split.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: Backtrack over every possible next-piece length at each position, skipping any piece already used in the current path, and track the best split size found.

test_cases.explanation: One optimal split is a, b, ab, c, cc -- 5 unique pieces.
Only 2 unique pieces are achievable, e.g. a, ba.
Splitting into a, a repeats a piece -- only 'aa' as one piece is forced.

title: Path with Maximum Gold
description: In a gold mine `grid`, each cell holds an amount of gold (0 means no gold, an empty/impassable cell). Starting from any cell with gold, collect the maximum amount of gold by moving in 4 directions, never revisiting a cell (and never entering a cell with 0 gold). Return the maximum gold collectible.
hints: Try starting a DFS from every gold cell; mark a cell visited by temporarily zeroing it out (so it can't be revisited), explore all 4 directions, then restore it before backtracking to try a different path.

test_cases.explanation: The best path 9->8->7 collects 24 gold.

title: K-th Lexicographical String of All Happy Strings of Length n
description: A string is happy if it consists only of letters 'a', 'b', 'c' and no two adjacent characters are equal. There are exactly `3 * 2^(n-1)` happy strings of length `n`; consider them sorted lexicographically. Return the k-th one (1-indexed), or an empty string if there are fewer than `k` happy strings of that length.
hints: Build the string character by character, trying 'a' then 'b' then 'c' at each position (skipping whatever equals the previous character) -- this generates happy strings in exactly lexicographic order, so just stop at the k-th one generated.

test_cases.explanation: The 3 length-1 happy strings are a, b, c -- the 3rd is c.
Only 3*2^1=6 happy strings of length 2 exist, so k=7 is out of range.

title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
description: Given an integer array `arr` and an integer `difference`, return the length of the longest subsequence in `arr` that forms an arithmetic sequence with the exact common difference `difference`.
hints: dp[v] = length of the best qualifying subsequence ENDING in value v. Scanning left to right, dp[arr[i]] = dp.get(arr[i] - difference, 0) + 1 -- an O(n) single hash-map pass.

test_cases.explanation: The whole array is already an arithmetic sequence with difference 1.
No two consecutive elements differ by exactly 1.

title: Count Different Palindromic Subsequences
description: Given a string `s`, return the number of DIFFERENT (distinct as strings) non-empty palindromic subsequences it contains, modulo 10^9 + 7.
hints: Interval DP over dp[i][j] = count of distinct palindromic subsequences in s[i..j].

When s[i] == s[j] == c, the count is 2*dp[i+1][j-1] (once with c on each end, once without) plus a correction depending on whether c appears again strictly inside (i+1..j-1): add 2 if never, add 1 if exactly once (avoiding double count of the single-c palindrome), or subtract the innermost overlap if it appears more than once.

test_cases.explanation: The 6 distinct palindromic subsequences are b, c, bb, cc, bcb, bccb.
No two characters repeat, so only the 4 single letters qualify.

title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together
description: Given a binary array `nums`, return the minimum number of swaps needed to group all the 1's present in the array together, in any position in the array.
hints: The final block of grouped 1's will have a fixed length equal to the total count of 1's -- slide a window of exactly that length across the array, and the answer is that length minus the maximum number of 1's any such window already contains.

test_cases.explanation: A window of length 3 (total ones) already containing 2 ones needs just 1 swap.
The single 1 is already 'grouped' by itself.

title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together II
description: Same setup as before, but `nums` is now CIRCULAR (the last element is adjacent to the first). Given a binary circular array `nums`, return the minimum number of swaps needed to group all the 1's together anywhere in the circle.
hints: Same sliding-window idea as the linear version, but the window of length (count of ones) now needs to wrap around the end of the array back to the start -- index with modulo n instead of stopping at the boundary.

test_cases.explanation: Wrapping the window around the end, one window already has 2 of the 3 ones.
Wrapping around, positions 4,0,1 already hold all three 1's together.

title: String Compression
description: Given an array of characters `chars`, compress it in place using run-length encoding: each group of consecutive repeating characters becomes that character followed by its count (the count is omitted for a group of length 1). Return the resulting compressed string.
constraints: chars[i] is a lowercase or uppercase English letter.
hints: Scan through with two pointers, finding the extent of each run of identical characters, and append the character (and its count, if more than 1) to the result.

test_cases.explanation: Three runs: aa -> a2, bb -> b2, ccc -> c3.
A run of length 1 has no count appended.

title: Unique Morse Code Words
description: Each lowercase letter maps to a fixed Morse code string (a='.-', b='-...', ..., using the standard International Morse Code alphabet). A word's Morse "transformation" is the concatenation of its letters' Morse codes. Given an array of words, return the number of DIFFERENT transformations among all the words.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Build each word's Morse transformation and count how many distinct strings result (a hash set is the natural fit).

test_cases.explanation: 'gin' and 'zen' both transform to '--...-.', while 'gig' and 'msg' are each unique -- 3 distinct transformations.
Different letter orders give different transformations.

title: Groups of Special-Equivalent Strings
description: You may swap any two characters at even indices with each other, or any two characters at odd indices with each other, any number of times. Two strings are special-equivalent if one can be transformed into the other this way. Given an array of equal-length strings `words`, return the number of groups of special-equivalent strings.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
All words have the same length.
hints: Since any permutation is achievable within the even positions (and independently within the odd positions), a canonical key is (sorted even-indexed characters, sorted odd-indexed characters) -- count the distinct keys.

test_cases.explanation: The first three words share the key (ac,bd) sorted; the last three share (xz,zy) sorted -- 2 groups.

title: Number of Matching Subsequences
description: Given a string `s` and an array of strings `words`, return the number of strings in `words` that are subsequences of `s` (formed by deleting zero or more characters from `s` without reordering the rest).
constraints: s and words[i] consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Checking each word against s independently with a two-pointer walk (or Python's `all(ch in it for ch in w)` idiom over an iterator of s) already runs comfortably within the limits here.

test_cases.explanation: 'a', 'acd', and 'ace' are all subsequences of 'abcde'; 'bb' is not (only one b exists).

title: Camelcase Matching
description: Given an array of strings `queries` and a string `pattern`, return an array of booleans where the i-th entry is true if `queries[i]` matches `pattern`: `queries[i]` matches `pattern` if you can insert lowercase letters (zero or more, anywhere) into `pattern` to make it equal to `queries[i]` (uppercase letters cannot be inserted or skipped, so every uppercase letter in `queries[i]` must correspond exactly, in order, to an uppercase letter in `pattern`).
constraints: queries[i] and pattern consist of English letters.
hints: Two pointers per query: walk through the query; if the current query character matches the next unconsumed pattern character, advance the pattern pointer, otherwise the query character must be lowercase (an inserted letter) or the match fails.

test_cases.explanation: 'FooBar', 'FootBall', and 'FrameBuffer' each insert only lowercase letters around F...B. 'FooBarTest' fails on the extra uppercase 'T', and 'ForceFeedBack' fails on its extra uppercase 'F' -- uppercase letters can never be inserted.
Uppercase letters in pattern must appear in the query too.

title: Minimum Number of Frogs Croaking
description: Each frog croaks the exact sequence 'croak', one letter at a time, and different frogs' letters may interleave in the input string `croakOfFrogs`. Return the minimum number of distinct frogs needed to produce `croakOfFrogs` in that exact letter order, or -1 if the string could not have been produced this way (e.g. a letter arrives out of any valid sequence, or some frog is left mid-croak at the end).
hints: Track how many frogs are currently sitting at each letter of 'croak'. A 'c' either starts a new frog or reuses one that just finished (peak concurrent frogs is the answer); every other letter must advance an existing frog from the previous letter, or the string is invalid.

test_cases.explanation: One frog can croak twice in a row -- 1 frog suffices.
Two frogs croak with interleaved letters -- 2 frogs needed.
The letter sequence contains an invalid transition ('crook' has two o's in a row for that frog).

title: Reveal Cards In Increasing Order
description: You have a deck of cards with distinct values `deck`. Repeatedly perform: reveal the top card (and remove it from the deck), then move the new top card to the bottom of the deck (if any remain). Return an arrangement of `deck` (a permutation of its values) such that performing this process reveals the cards in strictly increasing order.
constraints: All the values in deck are unique.
hints: Simulate the process BACKWARD: with a queue of index positions 0..n-1, repeatedly place the next-smallest sorted value at the front index and rotate the following index to the back -- this reconstructs exactly which original position each sorted value must occupy.

test_cases.explanation: The classic seven-card example arrangement.
A single card is trivially revealed first.

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String II
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, repeatedly remove `k` adjacent and equal letters (this may create new adjacent-equal groups, which should also be removed) until no such removal is possible. Return the final string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: A stack of [character, run-length] pairs handles this in one pass: extend the top pair if it matches the current character, popping it entirely once its count hits k.

test_cases.explanation: 'eee' and 'ccc' both collapse first, then the resulting 'bb...bd' exposes... the final result is 'aa'.
'aaa' and 'bbb' both fully collapse, leaving nothing.
No adjacent duplicates exist at all.

title: Maximum Frequency Stack
description: A max frequency stack pushes values and, when popped, removes and returns the most frequent value currently in the stack (ties broken by removing the most recently pushed among the tied values). Given the sequence of operations `opTypes` (each "push" or "pop") applied in order, with `opVals[i]` giving the value to push for a "push" operation (ignored for "pop"), return an array of the values returned by each "pop" operation, in order.
constraints: Every "pop" is guaranteed to have at least one value available to remove.
hints: Keep each value's current frequency, and a stack of values PER frequency level (group[f] = values currently at frequency f, in push order).
A pop always takes from group[maxFreq]'s top; if that empties the group, maxFreq drops by one.

test_cases.explanation: 5 has frequency 3, the highest, so it's popped first; then 7 (freq 2, more recent than the other freq-2 tie); then 5 again; then 4.

title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
description: A stack of maximum size `maxSize` supports: "push" (add a value, ignored if the stack is already full), "pop" (remove and record the top value, or record -1 if empty), and "increment" (add a given amount to the bottom `k` elements of the stack, or to all of them if fewer than `k` exist). Given the operation sequence `ops` and their arguments `args` (`args[i] = [value]` for push, `[]` for pop, or `[k, val]` for increment), return an array of the values recorded by every "pop" operation, in order.
hints: A plain array/list as the stack works fine: push/pop from the end respecting maxSize, and increment just adds to the first k elements from the bottom (index 0 upward), capped at the stack's current size.

test_cases.explanation: The push of 4 is dropped (stack full at 3); increment(5,100) adds 100 to all 3 elements; increment(2,100) adds 100 to the bottom 2.
The second pop finds an empty stack, recording -1.
The second push is dropped since maxSize is 1.

title: Find the Difference
description: String `t` is formed by shuffling string `s` and then adding one extra random lowercase letter somewhere. Return that extra letter.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: XOR-ing every character code in both s and t together cancels out every letter that appears in both, leaving only the extra one (works even with repeated letters).

test_cases.explanation: 'e' is the added letter.
Even with a repeated letter, the extra 'a' is still found correctly.

title: Check If a Word Occurs As a Prefix of Any Word in a Sentence
description: Given a `sentence` (space-separated lowercase words) and a `searchWord`, return the 1-indexed position of the first word in `sentence` that has `searchWord` as a prefix, or -1 if no such word exists.
constraints: sentence consists of lowercase English letters and spaces.
searchWord consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Split the sentence into words and check each one's prefix in order, returning as soon as one matches (1-indexed).

test_cases.explanation: 'burger' is the 4th word and starts with 'burg'.

inputs.sentence: this problem is an easy problem

test_cases.explanation: The FIRST matching word (the 2nd word) is returned, even though a later word also matches.

title: Decode XORed Permutation
description: There is an integer permutation `perm` of the numbers 1 to n (n is guaranteed ODD). It was encoded into an array `encoded` of length n - 1, where `encoded[i] = perm[i] XOR perm[i + 1]`. Recover and return the original `perm`.
hints: The XOR of ALL n values 1..n is known. The XOR of every OTHER encoded value (encoded[1], encoded[3], ...) equals perm[0] XOR (all-values-XOR) -- because of how the odd-indexed differences telescope -- so XOR-ing those two together isolates perm[0].
Once perm[0] is known, every next value follows by XOR-ing with the corresponding encoded entry.

test_cases.explanation: A permutation of {1,2,3} with perm[0]^perm[1]=3 and perm[1]^perm[2]=1 is [1,2,3].

title: Largest Number After Digit Swaps by Parity
description: Given a positive integer `num`, you may swap any two digits that have the SAME parity (both odd or both even), any number of times. Return the largest possible value of `num` achievable this way.
hints: Since any same-parity digits can be freely rearranged among themselves, sort the odd digits descending and the even digits descending separately, then rebuild the number by filling each position from the appropriately-sorted pool based on that position's original parity.

test_cases.explanation: Odd digits {1,3} sorted desc -> 3,1; even digits {2,4} sorted desc -> 4,2; rebuilt as 3412.
All digits are even, so they can be fully sorted descending.

title: Reduce Array Size to the Half
description: You are given an integer array `arr`. You may remove elements by choosing a value and removing every occurrence of it. Return the minimum number of distinct values you must choose to remove so that at least half of the elements are gone.
hints: Greedily remove the value with the HIGHEST remaining frequency first -- sort frequencies descending and keep taking until the running removed-count reaches half the array.

test_cases.explanation: Removing 3 (4 copies) and 5 (3 copies) removes 7 of the 10 elements, already past half.
One value covers everything.
Every value is distinct with frequency 1, so 5 removals (half the values) are needed.

title: Minimum Deletions to Make Array Beautiful
description: An array is beautiful if its length is even and, when split into consecutive pairs, no pair has two equal values (i.e. `nums[i] != nums[i+1]` for every even index `i`). Given an array `nums`, return the minimum number of elements to delete (from anywhere) to make it beautiful.
hints: Greedily build a result by skipping any element equal to the last one KEPT so far (eliminating all adjacent duplicates); if what's left has odd length, drop its last element too.

test_cases.explanation: Dropping one of the two 1's leaves [1,2,3,5], which is already beautiful.
A single leftover element can't form a pair, so it must be dropped too.
Already beautiful -- no deletions needed.

title: Largest Triangle Area
description: Given an array of points `points` on the X-Y plane, return the area of the largest triangle that can be formed using any three of them.
constraints: All the given points are distinct.
hints: The area of a triangle from three points is half the absolute value of the cross product of two of its edge vectors (the shoelace formula) -- try every triple.

test_cases.explanation: The triangle (0,0),(0,2),(2,0) has the largest area, 2.0.

title: Valid Square
description: Given the coordinates of four points `p1`, `p2`, `p3`, `p4` on the X-Y plane (in no particular order), return true if they form a valid square (non-degenerate, positive side length).
constraints: Each point has exactly 2 integer coordinates.
hints: Compute all 6 pairwise squared distances among the 4 points. A valid square has exactly 4 equal smaller values (the sides) and 2 equal larger values (the diagonals) that equal exactly twice a side's squared length.

test_cases.explanation: The classic unit-square example, given in an unsorted order.
The fourth point is far off, breaking the square shape.
Two identical points collapse a side to zero length -- degenerate.

title: Projection Area of 3D Shapes
description: You are given an `n x n` grid where `grid[i][j]` is the height of a tower of unit cubes placed at that cell (0 means no cubes). Return the total area of the shadows (projections) cast on the XY-plane (top view), the YZ-plane (side view), and the XZ-plane (front view), summed together.
hints: Top area is just the count of non-zero cells.
Front area is the sum of each row's maximum height; side area is the sum of each column's maximum height.

test_cases.explanation: Top=4 non-zero cells, front=2+4=6 (row maxes), side=3+4=7 (col maxes) -- total 17.

title: Surface Area of 3D Shapes
description: You are given an `n x n` grid where `grid[i][j]` is the height of a tower of unit cubes placed at that cell (0 means no cubes; towers on adjacent cells are flush against each other where they overlap in height). Return the total surface area of all the shapes combined.
hints: Every non-empty cell always contributes 2 (top+bottom).
For each of its 4 sides, it contributes max(0, its height - the neighbor's height) -- a taller tower exposes the difference above its shorter neighbor (or its full height if there's no neighbor).

test_cases.explanation: A single 2-tall tower: 2 (top+bottom) + 4 sides of height 2 = 10.

title: Maximum Good People Based on Statements
description: There are `n` people, each either good (always tells the truth) or bad (may lie or tell the truth). You are given `statements`, an `n x n` grid where `statements[i][j] == 1` means person `i` says person `j` is good, `== 0` means person `i` says person `j` is bad, and `== 2` means person `i` made no statement about person `j`. Return the maximum possible number of good people consistent with the statements (a valid assignment requires every GOOD person's statements to all be true; bad people's statements are unconstrained).
hints: n is small enough (<=15) to brute-force every subset of 'who is good' as a bitmask.
A candidate assignment is valid only if every person marked good in it has ALL of their statements about others match that same assignment exactly.

test_cases.explanation: Persons 0 and 1 vouch for each other consistently, and person 2 can be bad -- 2 good people.
Each accuses the other of being bad -- at most 1 can be good.
No statements at all -- everyone can be good.

title: Minimum One Bit Operations to Make Integers Zero
description: Given an integer `n`, you may perform two kinds of operations: change the rightmost (least significant) bit, or change the i-th bit if the (i-1)-th bit is 1 and every bit before it (from position i-2 down to 0) is 0. Return the minimum number of operations needed to turn `n` into 0.
hints: This is really about converting n's binary representation between normal binary and reflected Gray code -- the minimum operation count has a neat closed form computable by repeatedly XOR-ing n with itself shifted right, accumulating the result.

test_cases.explanation: Already zero.

title: Count Triplets That Can Form Two Arrays of Equal XOR
description: Given an integer array `arr`, return the number of triplets `(i, k, j)` with `0 <= i < k < j < arr.length` such that the XOR of `arr[i..k-1]` equals the XOR of `arr[k..j-1]`.
hints: The two XOR'd segments are equal exactly when the XOR of the whole combined range arr[i..j-1] is 0, i.e. prefixXor[i] == prefixXor[j].
For each such pair (i, j), EVERY choice of k strictly between them is valid, contributing (j - i - 1) triplets at once.

test_cases.explanation: All C(5,2)-style valid (i,j) pairs contribute; the total is 4.

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
description: You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, both sorted in ascending order, and an integer `k`. Every pair `(nums1[i], nums2[j])` has a sum `nums1[i] + nums2[j]`. Return the `k` pairs with the smallest sums, ordered by sum ascending.
constraints: nums1 and nums2 are sorted ascending.
hints: Start a min-heap with the k best candidate pairs (nums1[i], nums2[0]) for i up to k -- the true smallest sum overall must be among these.
Each time you pop a pair (i, j), push its 'next' candidate (i, j+1) -- since nums2 is sorted, this always produces the next-best candidate from that i.

test_cases.explanation: The 3 smallest-sum pairs are [1,2], [1,4], [1,6].
Only 2 pairs exist in total, fewer than k=3.

title: Distant Barcodes
description: In a row of `n` barcodes `barcodes[i]`, rearrange the barcodes so that no two adjacent barcodes share the same value. Return any valid rearrangement; it is guaranteed one exists.
hints: Count frequencies and place the most frequent value first, filling every OTHER position (0, 2, 4, ...) before wrapping to fill the odd positions -- this spaces out the most common values as much as possible.

test_cases.explanation: 1 (frequency 3) fills positions 0,2,4 first; then 2,2,3 fill the rest.

title: Rearrange String k Distance Apart
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, rearrange its characters so that the same character appears at least `k` positions apart. Return any valid rearrangement, or an empty string if none exists.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Greedily place the currently-most-frequent character next (a max-heap by remaining count), then hold it in a cooldown queue until k characters have been placed since, at which point it becomes eligible again.

test_cases.explanation: One valid spacing is abcabc.
Three a's can never be spaced 3 apart within only 5 characters total.
k=0 means no spacing constraint at all.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Array Continuous
description: An array is continuous if, after sorting it, every pair of consecutive elements differs by exactly 1 (equivalently: all elements are distinct, and max - min == length - 1). In one operation you may replace any element with any value. Given an integer array `nums`, return the minimum number of operations to make it continuous.
hints: Elements you DON'T replace must already be distinct values that could sit inside some final window of n consecutive integers -- deduplicate and sort, then two-pointer to find the largest count of unique values within any window of width n.
The answer is n minus that largest count.

test_cases.explanation: Already continuous (2,3,4,5) -- 0 operations.
Keeping 1,2,3 (or replacing 1 with 4 to keep 2,3,5,6) needs 1 replacement.

title: Maximum Average Subarray II
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum average value of any contiguous subarray of length GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO `k`.
hints: Binary search on the answer x: subtract x from every element, and a subarray of length >= k with sum >= 0 in this shifted array exists exactly when the true average-x achievable is >= 0.
Checking that in O(n) uses a running prefix sum and the minimum prefix seen at least k steps back.

test_cases.explanation: The subarray [12,-5,-6,50,3] (length 5) averages 10.8, the best possible.
With k=1 the best is just the single largest element.

title: Minimum Operations to Make the Array K-Increasing
description: An array `arr` is k-increasing if `arr[i] <= arr[i + k]` for every valid `i` (comparing elements k apart). In one operation you may change any element to any value. Given an array `arr` and an integer `k`, return the minimum number of operations to make `arr` k-increasing.
hints: The condition only ever relates elements at the same position mod k -- split arr into k independent subsequences (indices 0,k,2k,...; 1,k+1,2k+1,...; etc).
Each subsequence needs to become non-decreasing with minimum changes, which is (its length) minus (its longest non-decreasing subsequence, found via patience sorting).

test_cases.explanation: The whole array must become non-decreasing; keeping just one element and changing the rest needs 4 operations.
Split into [4,5,6] and [1,2,2], both already non-decreasing -- 0 operations.

title: Count Subarrays With Median K
description: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers and an integer `k` known to be present in `nums`, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose median is exactly `k`. The median of a subarray of size `m` is the middle element after sorting if `m` is odd, or the LARGER of the two middle elements if `m` is even.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct.
hints: Every subarray must contain k itself. With this input size, checking every subarray directly (sort it, read off the median at index length//2 under this problem's even/odd convention) is simple and safely within limits.
For full efficiency on larger inputs: walk outward from k's position tracking a running 'more-than-k minus less-than-k' balance in both directions and combine counts with a hash map.

test_cases.explanation: The four subarrays [4], [1,4], [1,4,5], and [2,1,4,5] each have median 4.

title: Number of Subarrays with Bounded Maximum
description: Given an integer array `nums` and two integers `left` and `right`, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose maximum element is between `left` and `right`, inclusive.
hints: count(max in [left,right]) = count(max <= right) - count(max <= left-1).
count(max <= bound) is easy with a running streak: every element <= bound extends the current streak of valid subarrays ending here by 1 (an element above bound resets the streak to 0).

test_cases.explanation: The three qualifying subarrays are [2], [2,1], [3].
Every one of the 6 subarrays has max exactly 1.
No element even reaches the range, so no subarray qualifies.

title: Shortest Subarray to be Removed to Make Array Sorted
description: Given an integer array `arr`, remove one contiguous subarray (possibly empty) so that the remaining elements are sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the length of the shortest such subarray to remove.
hints: Find the longest already-sorted prefix and the longest already-sorted suffix.

If they already meet or overlap, the answer is 0. Otherwise, either remove everything between them (or past one end), or two-pointer merge across the prefix/suffix boundary to find a smaller removal that still leaves a valid sorted join.

test_cases.explanation: Removing [10,4,2] leaves [1,2,3,3,5], sorted -- length 3.
The whole array except one endpoint element must go.
Already sorted.

title: Filling Bookcase Shelves
description: You are placing books on a bookcase, in order, onto shelves of width `shelfWidth`. `books[i] = [thicknessi, heighti]`. You must place books left to right in the given order; when a shelf runs out of width for the next book, start a new shelf below it. The height of a shelf is the tallest book placed on it. Return the minimum possible total height of the bookcase.
hints: dp[i] = minimum height using the first i books. For each i, try ending the CURRENT shelf at every possible starting book j (walking backward while the accumulated thickness still fits), and take dp[j-1] + max height of books[j-1..i-1].

test_cases.explanation: The classic seven-book example, minimum total height 6.
Neither pair fits together -- each book needs its own shelf.

title: Minimum Number of Increments on Subarrays to Form a Target Array
description: You start with an integer array of the same length as `target`, all zeros. In one operation you may choose any contiguous subarray and increment every element in it by 1. Return the minimum number of operations needed to make the array equal to `target`.
hints: Think of it as filling a bar-chart skyline: an increment operation is a horizontal segment. The minimum number of segments needed equals the sum of every 'uphill' step target[i] - target[i-1] (only counting positive increases, with an implicit 0 before the first element).

test_cases.explanation: Building this triangular skyline takes 3 operations (nested ranges of widening then narrowing width).
One single operation covering the whole array suffices.

title: Shuffle String
description: Given a string `s` and an integer array `indices` of the same length, character `s[i]` belongs at position `indices[i]` in the final string. Return the shuffled string.
constraints: All values in indices are unique.
hints: Allocate a result array of the same length, and directly place each character at its target index.

test_cases.explanation: 'c' moves to index 4, 'o' to index 5, and so on, spelling 'leetcode'.

title: Concatenation of Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` of length `n`, return an array of length `2n` formed by concatenating `nums` with itself.
hints: Just append the array to a copy of itself.

title: Find Target Indices After Sorting Array
description: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, sort `nums` in ascending order and return the (0-indexed) indices where the value `target` occurs in the sorted array, in ascending order.
hints: Sort the array, then scan for every index holding target (or binary search for the first occurrence and count how many follow, since sorted arrays place equal values contiguously).

test_cases.explanation: Sorted, nums becomes [1,2,2,3,5] -- target 2 sits at indices 1 and 2.
4 never appears in nums.

title: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
description: The XOR total of an array is the XOR of all its elements (0 for an empty array). Given an array `nums`, return the sum of the XOR totals of every possible subset of `nums` (there are `2^n` subsets, including the empty one).
hints: With n <= 12 there are at most 4096 subsets -- enumerate every subset with a bitmask and sum their XOR totals directly.

title: Minimum Sum of Four Digit Number After Splitting Digits
description: Given a 4-digit positive integer `num`, split its digits into two new 2-digit numbers (using each original digit exactly once, in any grouping) and return the minimum possible sum of those two numbers.
hints: Sort the 4 digits ascending; pair the two smallest digits as the tens digits of the two new numbers, and the two largest as the ones digits, to keep both numbers as small as possible.

test_cases.explanation: Digits sorted: 2,2,3,9 -- tens get 2,2 and ones get 3,9, giving 23+29=52.

title: Maximum Difference Between Increasing Elements
description: Given a 0-indexed array `nums`, find the maximum value of `nums[j] - nums[i]` over all pairs with `i < j` and `nums[i] < nums[j]`. Return that maximum difference, or -1 if no such pair exists.
hints: Scan left to right tracking the smallest value seen so far; at each position, the best difference ending here is the current value minus that running minimum (only if it's positive).

test_cases.explanation: The best pair is (1,5), a difference of 4.
Every later element is smaller, so no increasing pair exists.

title: Rearrange Array Elements by Sign
description: Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of even length, containing exactly n/2 positive and n/2 negative integers, rearrange it so that positive and negative numbers alternate starting with a positive number, while preserving the relative order of the positive numbers among themselves and of the negative numbers among themselves. Return the rearranged array.
constraints: nums consists of equal numbers of positive and negative integers.
hints: Split nums into its positive and negative sub-sequences (each already in original relative order), then interleave them one from each list at a time.

test_cases.explanation: Positives in order [3,1,2], negatives in order [-2,-5,-4] -- interleaved: 3,-2,1,-5,2,-4.

title: Minimum Operations to Halve Array Sum
description: You are given an array `nums` of positive numbers. In one operation, choose any element and reduce it to exactly half its current value (it may become non-integer). Return the minimum number of operations needed so that the total sum of the array is reduced by at least half of its original sum.
hints: Greedily halve whichever element currently contributes the largest reduction -- a max-heap that lets you repeatedly halve and re-insert the top value is exactly what's needed.

test_cases.explanation: Halving 19 to 9.5, then 9.5 to 4.75, then 8 to 4 reduces the sum by 9.5+4.75+4=18.25, just past half of 33 (16.5).
The only element must be halved once.

title: Maximum Ice Cream Bars
description: You have `coins` total money and want to buy as many ice cream bars as possible; `costs[i]` is the price of the i-th bar, and each bar can only be bought once. Return the maximum number of ice cream bars you can buy without exceeding your budget.
hints: Buying the cheapest bars first always leaves room for the maximum count -- sort ascending and buy greedily until the budget runs out.

test_cases.explanation: Buying the two 1's and the 2 costs 4, leaving 3 which just covers the last 3-cost bar -- 4 bars total.
Even the cheapest bar (6) is unaffordable.

title: Minimum Cost to Buy Candies With Discount
description: A store offers a deal: for every 3 candies you buy, the cheapest of the three is free (you must actually select all three together to claim the discount). Given an array `cost` of candy prices, return the minimum total amount of money needed to buy all the candies.
hints: Sort prices descending and group into threes: the third (cheapest) item in every group of 3 is free -- so skip paying for every index at position 2, 5, 8, ... in that sorted order.

test_cases.explanation: Sorted descending 3,2,1 -- the cheapest (1) is free, paying 3+2=5.
Fewer than 3 candies -- no discount applies.

title: Number of Days Between Two Dates
description: Given two dates `date1` and `date2`, each formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD", return the number of days between them.
constraints: The given dates are valid dates between the years 1971 and 2100.
hints: Convert each date to a day-count since some fixed epoch (accounting correctly for leap years -- divisible by 4, except centuries unless divisible by 400), then take the absolute difference.

test_cases.explanation: The same date is 0 days apart.
Spans several leap years (including the year-2000 special case, which IS a leap year since it's divisible by 400).

title: Day of the Week
description: Given a date as `day`, `month`, and `year` (a valid date between 1971 and 2100), return the name of the day of the week it falls on ("Monday", "Tuesday", etc.).
constraints: The given date is valid between 1971-01-01 and 2100-12-31.
hints: Use Zeller's congruence (or equivalently count total days elapsed since a known reference date, accounting for leap years) to compute the weekday directly.

title: Sum of Digits of String After Convert
description: Given a lowercase string `s` and an integer `k`: first, convert `s` to an integer by replacing every letter with its 1-indexed position in the alphabet (a=1, b=2, ..., z=26) and concatenating those numbers together. Then, `k` times in a row, replace the current integer with the sum of its digits. Return the final integer after these `k` transformations.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
The resulting integer will fit within a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Build the big concatenated digit string first, then repeat 'sum of digits' k times -- after the very first sum, the value is already small, so the remaining repeats are cheap.

test_cases.explanation: 'i' is the 9th letter, so the concatenated number is 9999, whose digit sum is 36.
1 (the code for 'a') stays 1 through any number of digit-sum passes.

title: Special Array With X Elements Greater Than or Equal X
description: An array `nums` is special if there exists a number `x` such that exactly `x` elements of `nums` are greater than or equal to `x` (x need not be an element of `nums`). Given `nums`, return that value `x`, or -1 if no such (necessarily unique) value exists.
hints: Try every candidate x from 0 to n (the array length) -- for each, count how many elements are >= x and check if it equals x exactly.

test_cases.explanation: Exactly 2 elements (3 and 5) are >= 2.
x=0 would need 0 elements >= 0, but every element counts as >=0 (giving a count of 2), and no other x works either -- no valid x exists.

title: Maximum Product Difference Between Two Pairs
description: The product difference of a pair of numbers `(a, b)` and a pair `(c, d)` is `a * b - c * d`. Given an integer array `nums` of at least 4 elements, choose 4 distinct indices to form two pairs and return the maximum possible product difference.
hints: The maximum product comes from the two largest values; the minimum product comes from the two smallest -- sort and take the difference of those two products directly.

test_cases.explanation: 7*6=42 (largest pair) minus 2*4=8 (smallest pair) gives 34.

title: Find the Winner of the Circular Game
description: There are `n` friends numbered 1 to n standing in a circle, playing a game: starting from friend 1 and counting clockwise, every `k`-th friend is eliminated (counting restarts from the friend right after the one just eliminated); the last friend remaining wins. Return the winner's number.
hints: This is the classic Josephus problem -- it has a simple O(n) recursive formula: the winner's 0-indexed position among m players is (winner among m-1 players + k) mod m, building up from 1 player (position 0).

test_cases.explanation: Eliminated in order: 2,4,1,5 -- friend 3 wins.
A single friend wins by default.
Counting every 1st friend eliminates 1, then 2, leaving 3.

title: Count Elements With Strictly Smaller and Greater Elements
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of elements that have BOTH a strictly smaller element and a strictly greater element somewhere else in the array.
hints: An element qualifies exactly when it is neither the array's minimum nor its maximum -- find those two bounds once, then count elements strictly between them.

test_cases.explanation: 7 and 11 each have something smaller (2) and something larger (15) -- 2 and 15 themselves are the array's min and max, so neither qualifies.
All elements are equal -- none has anything strictly smaller or greater.

title: Minimum Difference Between Largest and Smallest Value in Three Moves
description: Given an integer array `nums`, in one move you may choose any element and change it to any value. Using at most 3 moves, return the minimum possible difference between the largest and smallest values in the array.
hints: If there are 4 or fewer elements, all of them can be changed to the same value, giving 0.

Otherwise, sort the array: the optimal strategy always removes some prefix of the smallest values and the complementary suffix of the largest values (totaling exactly 3 removed) -- try all 4 ways to split those 3 removals between the two ends.

test_cases.explanation: 4 or fewer elements -- change them all to match, difference 0.
Changing 0 and 14 (or 10,14) to match the middle values minimizes the spread to 1.
